hook: SCP-100 is a quiet one: a run-down scrapyard in South Carolina and the metal figure that still keeps it open for business. There is no body count here. Read it slowly, paying attention to the daily timetable and to the small names welded onto things, because the article does most of its talking through those details.
whyItMatters:
This is a good example of a file where the containment problem is barely a problem at all. The Foundation's biggest leverage is taking away two pet-like constructs, and its main worry is that passing drivers might stop to shop.

The piece shows how much character a report can carry without dialogue. The entity cannot speak or write, so everything we learn about it comes from its schedule, its cheating at the scales, and how it treats what it builds.
thingsToNotice:
The hourly routine reads like the working day of a small-business owner who also keeps pets and sits at a desk all night, and the rigged scales and the no-refunds sign make it a petty shopkeeper rather than a monster; it even sells constructs it knows will go dead once they pass the fence.

The ending reframes all of it. The owner on record is Joseph Duval, the yard is named after a Joe, and the note left on the door is signed J.J. and sends customers to the assistant. In 2005 the construct builds its first human figure, small, detailed, stainless steel and marked J.J. on its back, and keeps it beside it on the counter; when the Foundation confiscates it, the construct sits unmoving in the residence for ten days, while the article never says where the owner went beyond the billing that stopped about three months before discovery.
